desc:
Given a binary search tree with distinct values and an integer key, delete the node holding key (if there is one) and return the resulting tree in the same level-order encoding.

Deletion rule. To delete a node: if it is a leaf, remove it; if it has exactly one child, replace the node by that child (the child's whole subtree moves up); if it has two children, copy into it the smallest value of its right subtree (its inorder successor) and then delete that smallest node from the right subtree, which by construction has at most one child. If the key is not in the tree nothing changes.

Following this rule exactly makes the resulting tree unique.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14] is the tree whose root 8 has children 3 and 10; node 3 has children 1 and 6; node 10 has no left child and right child 14.

Example 1

tree = [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13], key = 3
Output: [8,4,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,-1,7,13]
Node 3 has two children. Its right subtree is rooted at 6 and its smallest value is 4, so 3 becomes 4 and the old node 4 (a leaf) is removed.

Example 2

tree = [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13], key = 10
Output: [8,3,14,1,6,13,-1,-1,-1,4,7]
Node 10 has only a right child, so 14 (with its subtree) takes its place.

Example 3

tree = [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13], key = 99
Output: [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13]
The key is not present.
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000, all values distinct; the tree is a valid BST
hints: Treat the three cases separately: no child, one child, two children. The first two only need a pointer change at the parent.
When the node has two children you cannot simply drop it. Which value in the tree can take its place and still keep everything in the left subtree smaller and everything in the right subtree larger?

Walk down while remembering the parent to find the key. For two children, walk left from the right child to the smallest node, copy its value up, and let its right child take its place. Finish with a breadth-first dump that writes -1 for missing children and removes trailing -1s.
editorial: Find the node with a normal BST search, remembering its parent so a link can be redirected. A leaf is detached by clearing the parent's link (or by emptying the tree when it is the root). A node with one child is bypassed: the parent links straight to that child. A node with two children is the interesting case: the smallest node of its right subtree is larger than everything on the left and not larger than anything on the right, so its value can be copied into the node. That smallest node has no left child, so detaching it falls back to the one-child case.

Finally serialise: a queue-based breadth-first walk writes each node's value and queues both children, with a placeholder for a missing child that prints as -1 and has no children of its own; trailing -1 entries are trimmed. Searching and fixing links is O(h); decoding and encoding the array make the total O(n) time and space.
